properties.Remarks: The shifting of eruption centers on Gamkonora, the highest peak of Halmahera, has produced an elongated series of summit craters along a N-S trending rift. Youthful-looking lava flows originate near the cones of Gunung Alon and Popolojo, south of Gamkonora. Since its first recorded eruption in the 16th century, typical activity has been small-to-moderate explosive eruptions. Its largest recorded eruption, in 1673, was accompanied by tsunamis that inundated villages.
properties.VPImageCaption: Gamkonora volcano, seen here from the NW coast near Gamsungi village, is one of Halmahera's more active volcanoes.  The summit crater of Gamkonora is elongated in a N-S direction, with a small crater lake at the north end.  The first two historical eruptions, in 1564 or 1565, and in 1693, were the most severe, producing respectively a destructive lava flow that reached the sea, and a tsunami that inundated villages.
properties.VPImageCredit: Photo by A. Solihin, 1984 (Volcanological Survey of Indonesia).
properties.Report_Name: Gamkonora (Indonesia) - Report for 5 November-11 November 2026 - New Unrest
properties.Report_Summary:
The Pusat Vulkanologi dan Mitigasi Bencana Geologi (PVMBG) reported increased seismicity at Gamkonora during October-November. According to a news article seismicity during the month of October was characterized by 129 tornillo earthquakes, five low-frequency earthquakes, 28 shallow volcanic earthquakes, and 79 deep volcanic earthquakes; there were increases in the daily average of shallow volcanic earthquakes from less than two to nine per day and in the daily average of deep volcanic earthquakes from less than four to five per day. During 1-5 November the seismic network recorded 13 tornillo earthquakes, three low-frequency earthquakes, one shallow volcanic earthquake, and eight deep volcanic earthquakes. PVMBG raised the Alert Level to 2 (on a scale of 1-4) at 1600 on 6 November due to the increased seismicity and warned the public to stay 2 km away from the summit. The volcano was closed to climbers.  
 Sources: Antara News,Pusat Vulkanologi dan Mitigasi Bencana Geologi (PVMBG, also known as CVGHM)
properties.Report_Source: Smithsonian / USGS Weekly Volcanic Activity Report

properties.Remarks: Symmetrical Mayon, which rises above the Albay Gulf NW of Legazpi City, is the most active volcano of the Philippines. The steep upper slopes are capped by a small summit crater. Recorded eruptions since 1616 CE range from Strombolian to basaltic Plinian, with cyclical activity beginning with basaltic eruptions, followed by longer periods of andesitic lava flows. Eruptions occur predominately from the central conduit and have also produced lava flows that travel far down the flanks. Pyroclastic density currents and mudflows have commonly swept down many of the approximately 40 ravines that radiate from the summit and have often damaged populated lowland areas. A violent eruption in 1814 killed more than 1,200 people and devastated several towns.
properties.VPImageCaption: Mayon in SE Luzon is one of the most active volcanoes in the Philippines. It rises above the Albay Gulf and is the result of eruptions from a single central conduit. Frequent eruptions have been recorded since 1616 and have typically included powerful explosive activity accompanied by pyroclastic flows, lahars, and lava flows that descended to the lower flanks.
properties.VPImageCredit: Photo by Kurt Fredrickson, 1968 (Smithsonian Institution).
properties.Report_Name: Mayon (Philippines) - Report for 5 November-11 November 2026 - New Eruptive Activity
properties.Report_Summary:
The Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS) reported additional details about the moderately explosive eruption that occurred at Mayon during 1153-1159 on 30 October. The eruption produced a dense, billowing, gray ash plume rapidly rose 3 km above the summit and drifted SW. Dense parts of the lower ash plume collapsed and generated small-volume pyroclastic density currents (PDCs) that traveled 1.5-2 km down the Bonga (SE) and Basud (E) drainages. Small-volume PDCs likely descended the flanks in other directions but were obscured by either weather or eruptive clouds. A pressure wave that was a maximum of 207 Pascals was detected by an infrasound station located 3 km SW of the crater and heard as a booming sound by residents within 13 km. A comparison of webcam images from before and after the eruption revealed significant topographic changes at the S crater rim and on the upper part of the Bonga drainage from an apparent build-up of lava spatter and pyroclastics. Incandescent lava on the S rim was visible during the evening of 30 October and occasionally produced incandescent rockfalls. Ash fell in a narrow swath to the SW. Minor amounts of ash fell in the barangay of Sua (Camalig), along with Maninila and Travesia (Guinobatan). A sulfur odor was reported in the barangays of Maninila and 18 (Legazpi City) and booming sounds were reported in Ligban (Camalig), Balogo (Oas), Travesia and Muladbucad Grande (Guinobatan), and 18.
  
During 5-11 November the seismic network recorded 2-20 daily volcanic earthquakes and 0-5 daily rockfalls. Sulfur dioxide emissions averaged 836-2,614 tonnes per day. Emissions rose as high as 1 km above the crater and drifted WNW, WSW, and SW; weather clouds obscured views on 8 November. Minor Strombolian activity was visible on 11 November. The Alert Level remained at 3 (on a 0-5 scale) and the public was reminded to stay away from the 6-km-radius Permanent Danger Zone (PDZ). 
 
 Sources: Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS) ,The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC)
properties.Report_Source: Smithsonian / USGS Weekly Volcanic Activity Report

properties.Remarks: The compound volcano of Nevados de Chillán is one of the most active of the Central Andes. Three late-Pleistocene to Holocene stratovolcanoes were constructed along a NNW-SSE line within three nested Pleistocene calderas, which produced ignimbrite sheets extending more than 100 km into the Central Depression of Chile. The dominantly andesitic Cerro Blanco (Volcán Nevado) stratovolcano is located at the NW end of the massif. Volcán Viejo (Volcán Chillán), which was the main active vent during the 17th-19th centuries, occupies the SE end. The Volcán Nuevo lava-dome complex formed during 1906-1945 on the NW flank of Viejo. The Volcán Arrau dome complex was then constructed on the SE side of Volcán Nuevo between 1973 and 1986, and eventually exceeded its height. Smaller domes or cones are present in the 5-km valley between the two major edifices.
properties.VPImageCaption: Volcán Nuevo, the newest cone of the three-peaked Nevados de Chillán volcano, was formed beginning in 1861.  It grew between Cerro Blanco and Volcán Viejo, which anchor the NW and SE ends of the complex, respectively.  Volcán Nuevo has been the most active volcano of the complex since its birth.  In 1973, the year of this photo, a long-term eruption began on the SE flank of Volcán Nuevo, producing a cone that by 1987 had grown above Volcán Nuevo.  Nevados de Chillán is one of the most active volcanoes of the Central Andes of Chile.
properties.VPImageCredit: Photo by Hugo Moreno, 1973 (University of Chile).
properties.Report_Name: Nevados de Chillan (Chile) - Report for 5 November-11 November 2026 - New Eruptive Activity
properties.Report_Summary:
The eruption at Nevados de Chillán was ongoing during 5-11 November based on reports from the Servicio Nacional de Geología y Minería (SERNAGEOMIN), the Servicio Geológico Minero Argentino (SEGEMAR), and the Buenos Aires Volcanic Ash Advisory Center (VAAC). On 8 November the Buenos Aires VAAC reported that a period of continuous ash emissions were identified in satellite images rising to 4.6 km (15,000 ft) a.s.l. and drifting SW. SERNAGEOMIN noted that two ash-and-gas plumes were visible in webcam images rising 2.3-2.4 km above the crater rim at 1854 and 1936 on 10 November. The plumes were generated by explosions associated with long-period (LP) volcanic events. The Alert Level remained at Estados de Actividad Volcánica (EAV) 3 (on a scale of 0-5). SEGEMAR maintained Alert Level Yellow (the second lowest level on a four-color scale). The Sistema y Servicio Nacional de Prevención y Repuesta Ante Desastres (SENAPRED) maintained an ?Preventive Early Alert? for Pinto and Coihueco and warned the public to stay 2 km away from Emission Center 3 (EC3). 
 Sources: Buenos Aires Volcanic Ash Advisory Center (VAAC) ,Servicio Geológico Minero Argentino (SEGEMAR),Servicio Nacional de Geología y Minería (SERNAGEOMIN),Sistema y Servicio Nacional de Prevención y Repuesta Ante Desastres (SENAPRED)
properties.Report_Source: Smithsonian / USGS Weekly Volcanic Activity Report

properties.Remarks: The 16-km-wide Tengger caldera is located at the northern end of a volcanic massif extending from Semeru volcano. The massive volcanic complex dates back to about 820,000 years ago and consists of five overlapping stratovolcanoes, each truncated by a caldera. Lava domes, pyroclastic cones, and a maar occupy the flanks of the massif. The Ngadisari caldera at the NE end of the complex formed about 150,000 years ago and is now drained through the Sapikerep valley. The most recent of the calderas is the 9 x 10 km wide Sandsea caldera at the SW end of the complex, which formed incrementally during the late Pleistocene and early Holocene. An overlapping cluster of post-caldera cones was constructed on the floor of the Sandsea caldera within the past several thousand years. The youngest of these is Bromo, one of Java's most active and most frequently visited volcanoes.
properties.VPImageCaption: Bromo volcano produces a gas-and-steam plume at the left in this view from the rim of Ngadisari caldera, the older of two Tengger calderas. Bromo and Batok in the lower center are two of several post-caldera cones within the caldera. The towering peak of Semeru appears in the background at the end of a N-S trending volcanic massif.
properties.VPImageCredit: Photo courtesy of Volcanological Survey of Indonesia.
properties.Report_Name: Tengger Caldera (Indonesia) - Report for 5 November-11 November 2026 - New Eruptive Activity
properties.Report_Summary:
The Pusat Vulkanologi dan Mitigasi Bencana Geologi (PVMBG) reported that at 1711 on 5 November a white-and-gray ash plume rose 500 m above the crater rim of Tengger Caldera?s Bromo cone and drifted W. The event lasted for 46 seconds based on seismic data. White steam-and-gas plumes rose as high as 600 m above the crater rim and drifted in various directions during 4-11 November. The Alert Level remained at 2 (on a scale of 1-4), and visitors were warned to stay outside of a 1-km radius of the crater. 
 Source: Pusat Vulkanologi dan Mitigasi Bencana Geologi (PVMBG, also known as CVGHM)
properties.Report_Source: Smithsonian / USGS Weekly Volcanic Activity Report

properties.Remarks: The Aira caldera in the northern half of Kagoshima Bay contains the post-caldera Sakurajima volcano, one of Japan's most active. Eruption of the voluminous Ito pyroclastic flow accompanied formation of the 17 x 23 km caldera about 22,000 years ago. The smaller Wakamiko caldera was formed during the early Holocene in the NE corner of the caldera, along with several post-caldera cones. The construction of Sakurajima began about 13,000 years ago on the southern rim and built an island that was joined to the Osumi Peninsula during the major explosive and effusive eruption of 1914. Activity at the Kitadake summit cone ended about 4,850 years ago, after which eruptions took place at Minamidake. Frequent eruptions since the 8th century have deposited ash on the city of Kagoshima, located across Kagoshima Bay only 8 km from the summit. The largest recorded eruption took place during 1471-76.
properties.VPImageCaption: A plume rises above the Minamidake crater on Sakurajima. Activity at Kitadake, the peak to the right in this view from the SE, ended about 4,850 years ago, after which eruptions took place at Minamidake. Sakurajima is one of Japan's most active volcanoes and is a post-caldera cone in the Aira caldera at the northern half of Kagoshima Bay. Frequent historical eruptions have deposited ash across the bay on Kagoshima, one of Kyushu's largest cities.
properties.VPImageCredit: Copyrighted photo by Shun Nakano (Japanese Quaternary Volcanoes database, RIODB, http://riodb02.ibase.aist.go.jp/strata/VOL_JP/EN/index.htm and Geol Surv Japan, AIST, http://www.gsj.jp/).
properties.Report_Name: Aira (Japan) - Report for 5 November-11 November 2026 - Continuing Eruptive Activity
properties.Report_Summary:
The Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) reported ongoing eruptive activity at Minamidake Crater (Aira Caldera?s Sakurajima volcano) during 2-9 November. An eruptive event at 1111 on 3 November generated an ash plume that rose 1 km above the crater rim and drifted SE. An explosion at 2217 on 5 November produced an ash plume that rose 1.4 km above the crater rim and drifted SE. Large blocks were ejected 800-1,100 m from the vent. Very small eruptive events were recorded during 6-9 November. The Alert Level remained at 3 (on a 5-level scale), and the public was warned to be cautious within 1 km of both the Minimadake and Showa craters. 
 Source: Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA)
properties.Report_Source: Smithsonian / USGS Weekly Volcanic Activity Report

properties.Remarks: Akan is a 13 x 24 km caldera located immediately SW of Kussharo caldera in eastern Hokkaido. The elongated, irregular outline of the caldera rim reflects its incremental formation during major explosive eruptions from the early to mid-Pleistocene. There are four post-caldera stratovolcanoes, three at the SW end of the caldera and the other on the NE side. Conical Oakandake was frequently active during the Holocene. The 1-km-wide Nakamachineshiri crater of Meakandake was formed during a major pumice-and-scoria eruption about 13,500 years ago. The Meakandake group, composed of nine overlapping cones E of Lake Akan, has produced mild phreatic eruptions since the beginning of the 19th century. The main cone of Meakandake proper has a triple crater at its summit. Although recorded eruptions at Meakandake have consisted of minor phreatic explosions, four major magmatic eruptions with pyroclastic flows have also occurred during the Holocene.
properties.VPImageCaption: Oakandake, the largest post-caldera cone at Akan volcano, is seen here from the W across the Akan Caldera lake. It was constructed at the NE end of the 13 x 14 km caldera, opposite a cluster of stratovolcanoes at the SW end. Meakan in the SW group has been frequently active.
properties.VPImageCredit: Photo by Wataru Hirose, 1996 (Hokkaido University).
properties.Report_Name: Akan (Japan) - Report for 5 November-11 November 2026 - Continuing Unrest
properties.Report_Summary:
The Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) reported that no eruptions at Akan (also known as Meakan-dake, which means Meakan Peak) of the Akan volcanic complex were recorded after 15 March; unrest continued to decline. Sulfur dioxide emissions averaged 300-400 tons per day (t/d) during February-April but declined to 100-200 t/d starting in June. Steam-and-gas emissions also became less dense and vigorous. Seismicity began to decrease in June and was characterized as low in October. The Alert Level was lowered to 1 (the lowest level on a 5-level scale) at 1000 on 4 November.  
 Source: Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA)
properties.Report_Source: Smithsonian / USGS Weekly Volcanic Activity Report

properties.Remarks: The Great Sitkin volcano forms much of the northern side of Great Sitkin Island. A younger volcano capped by a small, 0.8 x 1.2 km ice-filled summit caldera was constructed within a large late-Pleistocene or early Holocene scarp formed by massive edifice failure that truncated an older edifice and produced a submarine debris avalanche. Deposits from this and an even older debris avalanche from a source to the south cover a broad area of the ocean floor north of the volcano. The summit lies along the eastern rim of the younger collapse scarp. Deposits from an earlier caldera-forming eruption of unknown age cover the flanks of the island to a depth up to 6 m. The small younger caldera was partially filled by lava domes emplaced in 1945 and 1974, and five small older flank lava domes, two of which lie on the coastline, were constructed along northwest- and NNW-trending lines. Hot springs, mud pots, and fumaroles occur near the head of Big Fox Creek, south of the volcano. Eruptions have been recorded since the late-19th century.
properties.VPImageCaption: Great Sitkin in the Andreanof Islands is seen here from Finger Bay on Adak Island. The edifice was constructed within a caldera, part of which forms the high snow-covered peak to the right. The post-caldera cone contains a 0.8 x 1.2 km ice-filled summit crater. The rim forms the irregular summit on the left horizon. A lava dome 400-600 m wide was emplaced through a glacier in 1945.
properties.VPImageCredit: Photo by Fred Zeillemaker, 1982 (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, courtesy of Alaska Volcano Observatory).
properties.Report_Name: Great Sitkin (United States) - Report for 5 November-11 November 2026 - Continuing Eruptive Activity
properties.Report_Summary:
The Alaska Volcano Observatory (AVO) reported that slow lava effusion continued to feed a thick flow in Great Sitkin?s summit crater during 4-9 November based on webcam and satellite images. The S flank of the dome slowly advanced and generated occasional small rockfalls. Minor earthquakes consistent with the growth of the lava dome were detected by the seismic network. Weather clouds obscured webcam and satellite views during most of the week, though warm surface temperatures over the active lava dome were identified in overnight satellite images during 7-8 November. The Volcano Alert Level remained at Watch (the third level on a four-level scale) and the Aviation Color Code remained at Orange (the third color on a four-color scale). AVO moved from daily to weekly updates on 9 November.  
 Source: US Geological Survey Alaska Volcano Observatory (AVO)
properties.Report_Source: Smithsonian / USGS Weekly Volcanic Activity Report

properties.Remarks: The truncated summit of Gunung Ibu stratovolcano along the NW coast of Halmahera Island has large nested summit craters. The inner crater, 1 km wide and 400 m deep, has contained several small crater lakes. The 1.2-km-wide outer crater is breached on the N, creating a steep-walled valley. A large cone grew ENE of the summit, and a smaller one to the WSW has fed a lava flow down the W flank. A group of maars is located below the N and W flanks. The first observed and recorded eruption was a small explosion from the summit crater in 1911. Eruptive activity began again in December 1998, producing a lava dome that eventually covered much of the floor of the inner summit crater along with ongoing explosive ash emissions.
properties.VPImageCaption: Gunung Ibu volcano on the NW coast of Halmahera Island rises beyond a small village on its WNW flank.  The summit of the stratovolcano is truncated by nested craters; the inner crater, 1 km wide and 400 m deep, contains several small crater lakes.  The outer crater is breached on the north side, forming the deep valley seen here on the left side of the summit ridge. Few eruptions are known in historical time from Ibu, although it was erupting at the time of this February 1999 photo.
properties.VPImageCredit: Photo by Agus Karim, 1999 (Volcanological Survey of Indonesia).
properties.Report_Name: Ibu (Indonesia) - Report for 5 November-11 November 2026 - Continuing Eruptive Activity
properties.Report_Summary:
The Pusat Vulkanologi dan Mitigasi Bencana Geologi (PVMBG) reported that activity at Ibu continued during 5-11 November, with daily eruptive events recorded by the seismic network. Daily gray ash plumes rose 200-600 m above the summit and drifted in multiple directions. Incandescence at the summit was occasionally visible in webcam images. The Alert Level remained at 2 (the second lowest level on a four-level scale) and the public was advised to stay 2 km away from the active crater and 3.5 km away from the N crater wall opening. 
 Source: Pusat Vulkanologi dan Mitigasi Bencana Geologi (PVMBG, also known as CVGHM)
properties.Report_Source: Smithsonian / USGS Weekly Volcanic Activity Report

properties.Remarks: Karangetang (Api Siau) volcano lies at the northern end of the island of Siau, about 125 km NNE of the NE-most point of Sulawesi. The stratovolcano contains five summit craters along a N-S line. It is one of Indonesia's most active volcanoes, with more than 40 eruptions recorded since 1675 and many additional small eruptions that were not documented (Neumann van Padang, 1951). Twentieth-century eruptions have included frequent explosive activity sometimes accompanied by pyroclastic flows and lahars. Lava dome growth has occurred in the summit craters; collapse of lava flow fronts have produced pyroclastic flows.
properties.VPImageCaption: Karangetang (Api Siau) is one of Indonesia's most active volcanoes.  Twentieth-century eruptions have included frequent explosive activity that is sometimes accompanied by pyroclastic flows and lahars.  Lava dome growth has occurred in the summit craters; collapse of lava flow fronts has also produced pyroclastic flows.
properties.VPImageCredit: Photo by Volcanological Survey of Indonesia.
properties.Report_Name: Karangetang (Indonesia) - Report for 5 November-11 November 2026 - Continuing Eruptive Activity
properties.Report_Summary:
The Pusat Vulkanologi dan Mitigasi Bencana Geologi (PVMBG) reported that the eruption at Karangetang?s North Crater (Kawah Dua), characterized by the effusion of incandescent material, occasional small explosions, and periodic ash plumes, continued during 5-11 November. At 1314 on 5 November a dense white, gray, and brown ash plume rose 800 m above the summit and drifted S and SW. A dense white-and-gray ash plume rose 1 km above the summit and drifted SW at 1734 on 7 November. At 1914 on 9 November a dense white-and-gray ash plume rose 1 km above the summit and drifted NW. Incandescent material at the summit and on the flanks was visible in a webcam image at 1916. Rumbling sounds and occasional booms were reported during 8-11 November. According to news articles lava flows or incandescent avalanches of material traveled as far as 1 km S, SW, and W and 500-700 m NW. Incandescent material was ejected as high as 400 m above the summit. The Alert Level remained at 2 (on a scale of 1-4) and the public was advised to stay 1.5 km away from both craters, with an extension to 2.5 km on the NW and SW flanks of North Crater. 
 Sources: Antara News,Pusat Vulkanologi dan Mitigasi Bencana Geologi (PVMBG, also known as CVGHM)
properties.Report_Source: Smithsonian / USGS Weekly Volcanic Activity Report

properties.Remarks: Kilauea overlaps the E flank of the massive Mauna Loa shield volcano in the Island of Hawai`i. Eruptions are prominent in Polynesian legends; written documentation since 1820 records frequent summit and flank lava flow eruptions interspersed with periods of long-term lava lake activity at Halema`uma`u crater in the summit caldera until 1924. The 3 x 5 km caldera was formed in several stages about 1,500 years ago and during the 18th century; eruptions have also originated from the lengthy East and Southwest rift zones, which extend to the ocean in both directions. About 90% of the surface of the basaltic shield volcano is formed of lava flows less than about 1,100 years old; 70% of the surface is younger than 600 years. The long-term eruption from the East Rift Zone between 1983 and 2018 produced lava flows covering more than 100 km2, destroyed hundreds of houses, and added new coastline.
properties.VPImageCaption: This January 1968 photo of Halema‘uma‘u crater shows lava fountaining within the partly solidified crust of lava lake, and also overflowing below. This eruption began on 5 November 1967 and lasted until 13 July 1968.
properties.VPImageCredit: Photo by Richard Fiske, 1968 (Smithsonian Institution).
properties.Report_Name: Kilauea (United States) - Report for 5 November-11 November 2026 - Continuing Eruptive Activity
properties.Report_Summary:
The Hawaiian Volcano Observatory (HVO) reported that the eruption within Kilauea?s Kaluapele summit caldera, characterized by incandescence, intermittent spatter, lava fountaining, and lava flows from vents along the SW and W margins of Halema`um`u Crater, continued at variable levels during 4-11 November. During an overflight early on 4 November scientists observed roiling lava ponds in both the N and SW vents.
  

Sporadic large overflows occurred at the N vent and spattering and incandescence at the SW vent were visible overnight during 4-5 November. The overflows intensified at the N vent and during the late morning on 5 November there was a continuous low-level fountain. The fountain intensified and by 1210 fountaining episode 56 had begun. The fountain rapidly grew taller, reaching 200 m during 1330-1400. Lava descended the cone?s flanks in sheet-like flows and several long, channelized flows spread across the crater floor. Much of the W and N portions of the crater floor were covered with new lava, with flows reaching the E end of the crater. An eruption plume that rose as high as 5.5 km (18,000 ft) a.s.l. and drifted SW at lower levels and NW at upper levels. Trace amounts of Pele's hair fell W of the summit on Highway 11 and in the town of Pahala. The fountain began to decrease in height after 1400, fluctuated just before 1800, and then abruptly stopped at 1801, after around six hours of continuous fountaining. The average effusion rate during the fountaining was 200 cubic meters per second; the highest peak was 530 cubic meters per second. An estimated 6 million cubic meters of lava erupted. Lava on the crater floor continued to advance over the following hour. At 1450 on 6 November the Volcano Alert Level was lowered to Advisory (the second lowest level on a four-level scale) and the Aviation Color Code was lowered to Yellow (the second lowest color on a four-color scale). Incandescence at both the N and SW vents was variable during 7-110 November. Scientists observed roiling lava ponds 40-50 m deep within both vents during a helicopter overflight on 10 November.
 
 Source: US Geological Survey Hawaiian Volcano Observatory (HVO)
properties.Report_Source: Smithsonian / USGS Weekly Volcanic Activity Report

properties.Remarks: The Lewotolok (or Lewotolo) stratovolcano occupies the eastern end of an elongated peninsula extending north into the Flores Sea, connected to Lembata (formerly Lomblen) Island by a narrow isthmus. It is symmetrical when viewed from the north and east. A small cone with a 130-m-wide crater constructed at the SE side of a larger crater forms the volcano's high point. Many lava flows have reached the coastline. Eruptions recorded since 1660 have consisted of explosive activity from the summit crater.
properties.VPImageCaption: Lewotolo, seen here from the Flores Sea NW of the volcano, anchors the eastern end of the northern peninsula that is connected to Lomblen Island by a narrow isthmus.  Many lava flows have reached the coastline of the peninsula.  Historical eruptions from Lewotolo have been recorded since 1660 and have consisted of explosive activity from the summit crater.
properties.VPImageCredit: Photo by Rob McCaffrey, 1982 (Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute).
properties.Report_Name: Lewotolok (Indonesia) - Report for 5 November-11 November 2026 - Continuing Eruptive Activity
properties.Report_Summary:
The Pusat Vulkanologi dan Mitigasi Bencana Geologi (PVMBG) reported continuing eruptive activity at Lewotolok during 5-11 November. White-and-gray ash plumes rose as high as 100 m above the summit and drifted W and NW on 5 November, then as high as 300 m above the summit on 10 November with drifts NE, NW, and W. White plumes rose around 100 m above the summit on most other days. Webcam images showed incandescent material being ejected above the summit and onto the flanks on multiple days. The active lava flow on the SE flank was 600 m long. The Alert Level remained at 2 (on a scale of 1-4). The public was warned to stay 2 km away from the summit with an extension to 3 km on the S and SE flanks. 
 Source: Pusat Vulkanologi dan Mitigasi Bencana Geologi (PVMBG, also known as CVGHM)
properties.Report_Source: Smithsonian / USGS Weekly Volcanic Activity Report

properties.Remarks: Gunung Marapi, not to be confused with the better-known Merapi volcano on Java, is Sumatra's most active volcano. This massive complex stratovolcano rises 2 km above the Bukittinggi Plain in the Padang Highlands. A broad summit contains multiple partially overlapping craters constructed within the 1.4 km Bancah caldera. The summit craters are located along an ENE-WSW line, with volcanism migrating to the west. More than 50 eruptions, typically consisting of small-to-moderate explosive activity, have been recorded since the end of the 18th century; no lava flows outside the summit craters have been observed.
properties.VPImageCaption: Marapi, seen here in front of above rice fields, is Sumatra's most active volcano. More than 50 small-to-moderate explosive eruptions have occurred since the end of the 18th century. Marapi, not to be confused with the more well-known Merapi volcano on Java, has multiple summit craters and reaches 2,000 m above the Padang Highlands in central Sumatra.
properties.VPImageCredit: Photo by Amin, 2003 (Centre of Volcanology & Geological Hazard Mitigation, Volcanological Survey of Indonesia).
properties.Report_Name: Marapi (Indonesia) - Report for 5 November-11 November 2026 - Continuing Eruptive Activity
properties.Report_Summary:
The Pusat Vulkanologi dan Mitigasi Bencana Geologi (PVMBG) reported that activity at Marapi (on Sumatra) continued during 5-11 November. Eruptive events were recorded during 5, 7-8, and 12 November by the seismic network, but were not visually observed due to weather conditions and/or darkness. The Alert Level remained at 2 (on a scale of 1-4) and the public was warned to stay 3 km away from the active crater. 
 Source: Pusat Vulkanologi dan Mitigasi Bencana Geologi (PVMBG, also known as CVGHM)
properties.Report_Source: Smithsonian / USGS Weekly Volcanic Activity Report

properties.Remarks: Merapi, one of Indonesia's most active volcanoes, lies in one of the world's most densely populated areas and dominates the landscape immediately north of the major city of Yogyakarta. It is the youngest and southernmost of a volcanic chain extending NNW to Ungaran volcano. Growth of Old Merapi during the Pleistocene ended with major edifice collapse perhaps about 2,000 years ago, leaving a large arcuate scarp cutting the eroded older Batulawang volcano. Subsequent growth of the steep-sided Young Merapi edifice, its upper part unvegetated due to frequent activity, began SW of the earlier collapse scarp. Pyroclastic flows and lahars accompanying growth and collapse of the steep-sided active summit lava dome have devastated cultivated lands on the western-to-southern flanks and caused many fatalities.
properties.VPImageCaption: Merapi in central Java is capped by an unvegetated lava dome complex. The modern edifice of Merapi, to the left in this view, is constructed to the SE of the arcuate scarp on the right that was formed by destruction of the older Batulawang volcano. Periodic growth and collapse of lava domes produce pyroclastic flows (block-and-ash flows) and lahars that have devastated populated areas below the volcano.
properties.VPImageCredit: Photo by Yustinus Sulistiyo, 1994 (Volcanological Survey of Indonesia).
properties.Report_Name: Merapi (Indonesia) - Report for 5 November-11 November 2026 - Continuing Eruptive Activity
properties.Report_Summary:
The Pusat Vulkanologi dan Mitigasi Bencana Geologi (PVMBG) reported that the eruption at Merapi (on Java) continued during 5-11 November, with avalanches produced by the active lava dome on the upper SW flank. As many as four daily lava avalanches traveled as far as 2 km down Krasak and Sat/Putih drainages on the SW flank; weather conditions sometimes obscured views. The Alert Level remained at 3 (on a scale of 1-4), and the public was warned to stay 3-7 km away from the summit, based on location. 
 Source: Pusat Vulkanologi dan Mitigasi Bencana Geologi (PVMBG, also known as CVGHM)
properties.Report_Source: Smithsonian / USGS Weekly Volcanic Activity Report

properties.Remarks: Puracé is an active andesitic volcano with a 600-m-diameter summit crater at the NW end of the Los Coconucos Volcanic Chain. This volcanic complex includes nine composite and five monogenetic volcanoes, extending from the Puracé crater more than 6 km SE to the summit of Pan de Azúcar stratovolcano. The dacitic massif which the complex is built on extends about 13 km NW-SE and 10 km NE-SW. Frequent small to moderate explosive eruptions reported since 1816 CE have modified the morphology of the summit crater, with the largest eruptions in 1849, 1869, and 1885.
properties.VPImageCaption: Snow-capped Puracé volcano has a 500-m-wide summit crater and is one of the most active volcanoes in Colombia. Frequent explosive eruptions in the 19th and 20th centuries have modified the morphology of the summit crater, with some of the largest occurring in 1849, 1869, and 1885.
properties.VPImageCredit: Photo by Federmán Escobar Chávez, 2005.
properties.Report_Name: Purace (Colombia) - Report for 5 November-11 November 2026 - Continuing Eruptive Activity
properties.Report_Summary:
The Servicio Geológico Colombiano (SGC) reported that eruptive activity at Puracé continued during 3-9 November. Seismicity indicating fluid movement beneath Puracé and Piocollo volcanoes at depths less than 3 km was at similar levels to the previous week. Seismic signals related to rock-fracturing were located 12-18 km NE at depths of 7-11 km, beneath the Puracé and Piocollo volcanoes at depths of 1-3 km and had low magnitudes, and 4-6 km SE of Puracé at depths of 5-6 km. Sulfur dioxide and carbon dioxide levels were characterized as significant. Low-energy thermal anomalies on the Puracé crater floor were identified in satellite data. Continuous gas emissions and a total of 17 ash emissions were recorded. Plumes rose as high as 1.3 km above the summit of Puracé and drifted mainly NW. The Alert Level remained at Yellow (the second lowest level on a four-color scale). 
 Source: Servicio Geológico Colombiano (SGC)
properties.Report_Source: Smithsonian / USGS Weekly Volcanic Activity Report

properties.Remarks: Volcán El Reventador is the most frequently active of a chain of Ecuadorian volcanoes in the Cordillera Real, well east of the principal volcanic axis. The forested, dominantly andesitic stratovolcano has 4-km-wide avalanche scarp open to the E formed by edifice collapse. A young, unvegetated, cone rises from the amphitheater floor to a height comparable to the rim. It has been the source of numerous lava flows as well as explosive eruptions visible from Quito, about 90 km ESE. Frequent lahars in this region of heavy rainfall have left extensive deposits on the scarp slope. The largest recorded eruption took place in 2002, producing a 17-km-high eruption column, pyroclastic flows that traveled up to 8 km, and lava flows from summit and flank vents.
properties.VPImageCaption: A steam-and-gas plume rises from the central cone of Reventador volcano in this March 11, 2005 aerial view from the SE.  Several lava flows generated during eruptions in 2002 and 2004-2005 are visible on the south and SE flanks of the central cone.  The 3562-m-high central cone was constructed within the large 4-km-wide horseshoe-shaped caldera breached to the east (lower right).  The caldera was formed during a major collapse of the volcano, which produced a massive debris avalanche that swept into the Amazon basin.
properties.VPImageCredit: Photo by Patricio Ramon, 2005 (Instituto Geofisca, Escuela Politecnica Nacional).
properties.Report_Name: Reventador (Ecuador) - Report for 5 November-11 November 2026 - Continuing Eruptive Activity
properties.Report_Summary:
The Instituto Geofísico-Escuela Politécnica Nacional (IG-EPN) reported that eruptive activity at Reventador continued at a high level during 4-11 November. Seismicity included 63-89 daily explosions, long-period earthquakes, harmonic tremor, and tremor associated with emissions. Daily ash-and-gas plumes were visible in webcam images and reported by the Washington Volcanic Ash Advisory Center rising as high as 1.5 km above the crater rim and drifting in multiple directions. Incandescent blocks were visible during dark hours each day rolling as far as 1.1 km down the flanks. A pyroclastic flow descended the S flank on 18 October. The Secretaría de Gestión de Riesgos (SGR) maintained the Alert Level at Orange (the second highest level on a four-color scale). 
 Sources: Instituto Geofísico-Escuela Politécnica Nacional (IG-EPN) ,Secretaría de Gestión de Riesgos (SGR)
properties.Report_Source: Smithsonian / USGS Weekly Volcanic Activity Report

properties.Remarks: Rincón de la Vieja is a volcanic complex in the Guanacaste Range of NW Costa Rica. Sometimes referred to as the Rincon de la Vieja-Santa María Volcanic Complex, it consists of a slightly arcuate 20-km-long ridge of 12 craters and pyroclastic cones constructed within the 15-km-wide early Pleistocene Guachipelín caldera, whose rim is exposed on the south side. Sometimes known as the "Colossus of Guanacaste," it has an estimated volume of 130 km3 and contains at least nine major eruptive centers. The Santa María cone, the highest peak of the complex, is located on the E side of the ridge and has a lake within the 400-m-diameter crater. A Plinian eruption producing the 0.25 km3 Río Blanca tephra about 3,500 years ago was the last major magmatic eruption. All subsequent eruptions, including numerous reported eruptions possibly dating back to the 16th century, have been from the active crater, near the center of the complex, with an acidic 300-m-diameter lake.
properties.VPImageCaption: Part of the complex summit region of Rincón de la Vieja, the largest volcano in NW Costa Rica, is seen here from the north. Steam rises from the lake-filled Cráter Activo to the left, ENE of the Von Seebach cone (right). Laguna Fria (far-left) is not a crater lake, but a freshwater lake that formed between overlapping cones of the summit complex, which extends east and west beyond this area. Frequent eruptions from Cráter Activo have left surrounding terrain unvegetated.
properties.VPImageCredit: Photo by Federico Chavarria Kopper, 1999.
properties.Report_Name: Rincon de la Vieja (Costa Rica) - Report for 5 November-11 November 2026 - Continuing Eruptive Activity
properties.Report_Summary:
The Observatorio Vulcanologico y Sismologico de Costa Rica-Universidad Nacional (OVSICORI-UNA) reported that minor eruptive events at Rincón de la Vieja continued to be periodically detected by the seismic and infrasound network during 4-11 November. These eruptive events were sometimes accompanied by steam-and-gas plumes. One of the plumes rose as high as 1 km above the crater rim during the morning of 5 November. The Alert Level remained at Level 2, Yellow, the second lowest level on a four-level scale. 
 Source: Observatorio Vulcanologico y Sismologico de Costa Rica-Universidad Nacional (OVSICORI-UNA)
properties.Report_Source: Smithsonian / USGS Weekly Volcanic Activity Report

properties.Remarks: Sabancaya, located in the saddle NE of Ampato and SE of Hualca Hualca volcanoes, is the youngest of these volcanic centers and the only one to have erupted in historical time. The oldest of the three, Nevado Hualca Hualca, is of probable late-Pliocene to early Pleistocene age. The name Sabancaya (meaning "tongue of fire" in the Quechua language) first appeared in records in 1595 CE, suggesting activity prior to that date. Holocene activity has consisted of Plinian eruptions followed by emission of voluminous andesitic and dacitic lava flows, which form an extensive apron around the volcano on all sides but the south. Records of observed eruptions date back to 1750 CE.
properties.VPImageCaption: The Sabancaya volcanic complex consists of Sabancaya volcano proper (foreground), the older 6288-m-high Ampato volcano (background), and 6025-m Hualca Hualca volcano.  Sabancaya, viewed here from the NE, is constructed on the saddle between the two older volcanoes.  It is the youngest of the three Holocene volcanic centers and the only one to have erupted in historical time.  An extensive 15-km-wide apron of trachytic and dacitic lava flows surrounds the 5967-m-high volcano.  Records of historical eruptions date back to 1750.
properties.VPImageCredit: Photo by Norm Banks, 1988 (U.S. Geological Survey).
properties.Report_Name: Sabancaya (Peru) - Report for 5 November-11 November 2026 - Continuing Eruptive Activity
properties.Report_Summary:
The Instituto Geofísico del Perú?s (IGP) Centro Vulcanológico Nacional (CENVUL) reported continuing eruptive activity at Sabancaya during 2-8 November. The seismic network detected 17 seismic events associated with the movement of magmatic fluids, along with earthquakes indicating internal rock fracturing; no volcanic explosions occurred during the week. Gas, steam, and ash emissions periodically rose as high as 600 m above the summit and drifted less than 10 km SW and W. Moderate sulfur dioxide emissions averaged 535 tons per day, and five thermal anomalies (each 1 MW or less) associated with the lava dome were identified. The Alert Level remained at Orange (the third level on a four-color scale) and the public was warned to stay outside of a 12 km radius from the summit. 
 Source: Instituto Geofísico del Perú (IGP)
properties.Report_Source: Smithsonian / USGS Weekly Volcanic Activity Report

properties.Remarks: The isolated Sangay volcano, located east of the Andean crest, is the southernmost of Ecuador's volcanoes and its most active. The steep-sided, glacier-covered, dominantly andesitic volcano grew within the open calderas of two previous edifices which were destroyed by collapse to the east, producing large debris avalanches that reached the Amazonian lowlands. The modern edifice dates back to at least 14,000 years ago. It towers above the tropical jungle on the east side; on the other sides flat plains of ash have been eroded by heavy rains into steep-walled canyons up to 600 m deep. The earliest report of an eruption was in 1628. Almost continuous eruptions were reported from 1728 until 1916, and again from 1934 to the present. The almost constant activity has caused frequent changes to the morphology of the summit crater complex.
properties.VPImageCaption: The isolated Sangay volcano towers above tropical jungles east of the Andean crest.  Seen here from the NE, it is one of Ecuador's most active volcanoes and has been in frequent eruption during the past several centuries.  The steep-sided, glacier-covered volcano has been constructed within the older Verdeloma somma to the south.  Historical eruptions were first reported in 1628.  More-or-less continuous eruptions took place from 1728 until 1916, and again from 1934 until the present.
properties.VPImageCredit: Photo by Minard Hall, 1976 (Escuela Politécnica Nacional, Quito).
properties.Report_Name: Sangay (Ecuador) - Report for 5 November-11 November 2026 - Continuing Eruptive Activity
properties.Report_Summary:
The Instituto Geofísico-Escuela Politécnica Nacional (IG-EPN) reported that volcanic activity at Sangay continued during 4-11 November. The seismic network recorded 3-19 daily explosions, a few long-period earthquakes, a period of harmonic tremor, and 6-13 daily signals indicating emissions. On most days the Washington Volcanic Ash Advisory Center reported that ash-and-gas plumes were visible in webcam views and satellite images rising as high as 1.5 km above the crater rim and drifting mainly NW, W, and SW. During dark hours there were several episodes of incandescent material descending the flank as far as 500 m. Weather clouds sometimes prevented visual observations, especially during 8-10 November. The Secretaría de Gestión de Riesgos (SGR) maintained the Alert Level at Yellow (the second highest level on a four-color scale). The Secretaría de Gestión de Riesgos (SGR) maintained the Alert Level at Yellow (the second highest level on a four-color scale). 
 Sources: Instituto Geofísico-Escuela Politécnica Nacional (IG-EPN) ,Secretaría de Gestión de Riesgos (SGR)

properties.Remarks: Semeru, the highest volcano on Java, and one of its most active, lies at the southern end of a volcanic massif extending north to the Tengger caldera. The steep-sided volcano, also referred to as Mahameru (Great Mountain), rises above coastal plains to the south.  Gunung Semeru was constructed south of the overlapping Ajek-ajek and Jambangan calderas. A line of lake-filled maars was constructed along a N-S trend cutting through the summit, and cinder cones and lava domes occupy the eastern and NE flanks. Summit topography is complicated by the shifting of craters from NW to SE. Frequent 19th and 20th century eruptions were dominated by small-to-moderate explosions from the summit crater, with occasional lava flows and larger explosive eruptions accompanied by pyroclastic flows that have reached the lower flanks of the volcano.
properties.VPImageCaption: Semeru volcano rises above the coastal plain in Java, shown here producing a small ash plume in 1985. Larger eruptions occasionally produce pyroclastic flows and lahars that reach as far as the lower flanks of the volcano. Semeru (also known as Mahameru: "Great Mountain") has been in near-continuous activity since 1818.
properties.VPImageCredit: Photo by Tom Casadevall, 1985 (U.S. Geological Survey).
properties.Report_Name: Semeru (Indonesia) - Report for 5 November-11 November 2026 - Continuing Eruptive Activity
properties.Report_Summary:
The Pusat Vulkanologi dan Mitigasi Bencana Geologi (PVMBG) reported that activity continued at Semeru during 5-11 November, with daily eruptive events recorded by the seismic network. Plumes of variable combinations of white, gray, and black rose 100-1,000 m above the summit and drifted mainly S, SW, and W on most days; emissions were not visible due to weather conditions on 9 November. According to news articles multiple pyroclastic flows were recorded by the seismic network and/or visually observed descending the Kobokan drainage on the SE flank during 4-6 November. The first, recorded at 1249 on 4 November, was not visually observed due to weather conditions so the length was unknown. An eruptive event at 0633 on 5 November produced a dense gray ash plume that rose 700 m above the summit and drifted S and SW and a pyroclastic flow that traveled 3 km down the flank. A few hours later, at 0843, a dense gray ash plume rose 700 m and drifted S and SW and a pyroclastic flow that traveled 3.5 km down the flank. A gray-to-black ash plume rose 700 m above the summit and drifted SW at 0924 and a pyroclastic flow traveled 4.5 km down the flank. The next day, at 1548 on 6 November, a pyroclastic flow traveled 5 km down the flank and a white-and-gray ash plume rose 1 km above the summit and drifted SE. Around an hour later, at 1657, a dense gray ash plume rose 500 m above the summit and a pyroclastic flow traveled 4 km down the flank. On 6 November two people thought to be climbing Semeru on an unofficial route had not returned and were missing; search efforts continued at least through 10 November and the volcano remained closed to climbers. The Alert Level remained at 3 (the second highest level on a scale of 1-4) and the public was warned to stay at least 5 km away from the Jonggring Saloko Crater in all directions, 13 km from the summit on the SE flank along the Kobokan drainage, and 500 m from the banks of the Kobokan drainage as far as 17 km SE of the summit. 
 Sources: Antara News,Antara News,Antara News,Antara News,Pusat Vulkanologi dan Mitigasi Bencana Geologi (PVMBG, also known as CVGHM)
properties.Report_Source: Smithsonian / USGS Weekly Volcanic Activity Report

properties.Remarks: The high, isolated massif of Sheveluch volcano (also spelled Shiveluch) rises above the lowlands NNE of the Kliuchevskaya volcano group. The 1,300 km3 andesitic volcano is one of Kamchatka's largest and most active volcanic structures, with at least 60 large eruptions during the Holocene. The summit of roughly 65,000-year-old Stary Shiveluch is truncated by a broad 9-km-wide late-Pleistocene caldera breached to the south. Many lava domes occur on its outer flanks. The Molodoy Shiveluch lava dome complex was constructed during the Holocene within the large open caldera; Holocene lava dome extrusion also took place on the flanks of Stary Shiveluch. Widespread tephra layers from these eruptions have provided valuable time markers for dating volcanic events in Kamchatka. Frequent collapses of dome complexes, most recently in 1964, have produced debris avalanches whose deposits cover much of the floor of the breached caldera.
properties.VPImageCaption: Sheveluch has undergone several large flank collapse events to shape the edifice we see today. The frequent collapses of lava-dome complexes have produced numerous debris avalanches whose deposits cover much of the area south of the volcano. The light-colored hummocky deposits in the foreground were produced during the latest collapse in 1964.
properties.VPImageCredit: Photo by Kamchatka Volcanic Eruptions Response Team (courtesy of Dan Miller, U.S. Geological Survey).
properties.Report_Name: Sheveluch (Russia) - Report for 5 November-11 November 2026 - Continuing Eruptive Activity
properties.Report_Summary:
The Kamchatkan Volcanic Eruption Response Team (KVERT) reported continuing lava effusion and explosive activity at the lava domes along the N crater floor of Young Sheveluch (on the SW flank of Old Sheveluch) during 4-11 November. A thermal anomaly was identified in satellite images on most or all days. Explosions on 5 November produced ash plumes that rose 5.7 km (18,700 ft) a.s.l. and drifted 80 km ESE. On 8 November plumes of resuspended ash drifted 120 km E. Another ash plume on 10 November drifted 80 km NE. The Aviation Color Code remained at Orange (the second highest level on a four-color scale). Dates are based on UTC; specific events are in local time where noted. 
 Source: Kamchatkan Volcanic Eruption Response Team (KVERT)
properties.Report_Source: Smithsonian / USGS Weekly Volcanic Activity Report

properties.Remarks: The 8-km-long island of Suwanosejima in the northern Ryukyu Islands consists of an andesitic stratovolcano with two active summit craters. The summit is truncated by a large breached crater extending to the sea on the E flank that was formed by edifice collapse. One of Japan's most frequently active volcanoes, it was in a state of intermittent Strombolian activity from Otake, the NE summit crater, between 1949 and 1996, after which periods of inactivity lengthened. The largest recorded eruption took place in 1813-14, when thick scoria deposits covered residential areas, and the SW crater produced two lava flows that reached the western coast. At the end of the eruption the summit of Otake collapsed, forming a large debris avalanche and creating an open collapse scarp extending to the eastern coast. The island remained uninhabited for about 70 years after the 1813-1814 eruption. Lava flows reached the eastern coast of the island in 1884. Only about 50 people live on the island.
properties.VPImageCaption: A plume rises above Ontake, the summit crater of Suwanosejima. The 8-km-long island consists of a stratovolcano with two historically active summit craters. The dipping scarp at the top of the image opens towards the sea on the E flank and formed by edifice collapse. This is one of Japan's most frequently active volcanoes and has been in a state of intermittent Strombolian activity since 1949.
properties.VPImageCredit: Photo by Yukio Hayakawa, 1998 (Gunma University).
properties.Report_Name: Suwanosejima (Japan) - Report for 5 November-11 November 2026 - Continuing Eruptive Activity
properties.Report_Summary:
The Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) reported that eruptive activity at Suwanosejima?s Otake Crater continued during 30 October-6 November. Intermittent eruptive events produced ash plumes that rose as high as 500 m above the crater rim. The Alert Level remained at 2 (the second level on a five-level scale) and the public was warned to be cautious within 1.5 km of the crater. 
 Source: Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA)
